advances: Supplies a coarse-support separation argument for every uniformly bounded lattice-width class, including original laws with a small exceptional mass outside a bounded-width slab. Consequently, a countersequence to the unrestricted planar separation must avoid sufficiently high-mass bounded-width lattice slabs. An exact nonproduct family also refutes a uniform fourth-spatial-moment projection bound, even though its canonical KL divergence stays separated from zero. The unrestricted planar inverse is not proved or refuted here; the remaining case has no such coarse support concentration.

proof:
The function equal to \(e^{\boldsymbol\theta\cdot\mathbf x}/Z\) on \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\) and zero outside is finite-valued and globally log-concave. Completeness makes it agree with every lattice value of \(p\), including zeros, so the complete-table hypothesis of the declared canonical-array predecessor holds.

Use the canonical sampling representation of `464815b935df9890`: select a parity class \(\mathbf B\) with law \(\pi\), and, given \(\mathbf B\), select \(\mathbf X,\mathbf Y\) independently with law \(p\) conditioned on that class. Both unconditional endpoint laws are the original \(p\), and \(\mathbf J=(\mathbf X+\mathbf Y)/2\) has law \(\mathcal T(p)\). Completeness ensures \(\mathbf J\in D\). The sampling formula gives the displayed array directly and does not globally condition independent original endpoints on a parity match.

Let \(\mathbf m_{\mathbf b}=\mathbb E[\mathbf X\mid\mathbf B=\mathbf b]\). Conditional independence gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf m_{\mathbf B})\). Taking the covariance of the average, and then using the law of total covariance, proves the stated mean and covariance identities. If \(\mathcal T(p)=p\), the trace of their covariance difference vanishes. Each conditional covariance has nonnegative trace, and every occupied class has positive mass, so each conditional law is a point mass. Conversely, if each occupied class has only one site, then \(\mathbf X=\mathbf Y=\mathbf J\) almost surely, with any original weights. This proves the stationarity assertion for arbitrary weights and is not an application of the different stationarity theorem for \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}\).

For the log-affine root law, \(\log p_{\mathbf I}=\boldsymbol\theta\cdot\mathbf I-\log Z\) on \(D\). Mean preservation therefore gives \(\sum q^{\mathrm{can}}_{\mathbf J}\log p_{\mathbf J}=\sum p_{\mathbf I}\log p_{\mathbf I}\). Expanding relative entropy proves \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{\mathrm{can}}\|p)=H(p)-H(q^{\mathrm{can}})\), with no requirement that the common mean be integral.

We next establish a one-dimensional estimate, carefully distinguishing the two midpoint operations. Let \(\rho\) be a finitely supported log-concave law on an integer interval, put \(m=\max_j\rho_j\), and denote its two parity masses by \(\beta_0,\beta_1\). Let \(\rho^{\mathrm{can}}\) select its parity with probabilities \(\beta_b\) before averaging independent conditional endpoints. In contrast, \(\rho^{\mathrm{mid}}\) of `3a28e7b649873797` selects the parity with probabilities \(\beta_b^2/(\beta_0^2+\beta_1^2)\). Given the parity, their midpoint laws are identical. Hence

\[
\operatorname{TV}(\rho^{\mathrm{can}},\rho^{\mathrm{mid}})
\le\frac{\beta_0\beta_1|\beta_0-\beta_1|}{\beta_0^2+\beta_1^2}
\le\frac12|\beta_0-\beta_1|\le m.
\]

For the last inequality, a log-concave interval law is unimodal, so, including its exterior zeros, \(\sum_j|\rho_{j+1}-\rho_j|=2m\). Grouping even and odd neighbors gives \( |\beta_0-\beta_1|\le\sum_j|\rho_{2j}-\rho_{2j+1}|\le2m\). The preceding mixture calculation also holds when one parity mass is zero.

Item 2 of `3a28e7b649873797`, together with its Hellinger-to-total-variation comparison, gives \(\operatorname{TV}(\rho,\rho^{\mathrm{mid}})\ge\kappa a(\rho)\). Its off-diagonal probability is \(a(\rho)=1-\sum_j\rho_j^2/(\beta_0^2+\beta_1^2)\). Since the denominator is at least \(1/2\) and \(\sum\rho_j^2\le m\), the triangle inequality gives

\[
\operatorname{TV}(\rho,\rho^{\mathrm{can}})
\ge\kappa(1-2m)-m\ge\kappa-3m.
\]

An integral affine lattice bijection commutes with midpoint formation and permutes parity classes bijectively, because its linear part is invertible modulo two. It therefore carries the canonical array and row law to their corresponding pushforwards. Total variation, relative entropy, and the atomic moments are preserved. We may thus work in coordinates in which the first coordinate lies between zero and \(\omega\).

For each occupied first-coordinate row \(i\), let \(\alpha_i=\sum_jp_{(i,j)}\) and \(\rho^{(i)}_j=p_{(i,j)}/\alpha_i\). Completeness makes its positive support an integer interval, and log-affinity makes it a finite geometric law, hence log-concave. Define the auxiliary probability law \(\widehat q_{(i,j)}=\alpha_i\rho^{(i),\mathrm{can}}_j\), using canonical one-dimensional averaging separately in every row. This auxiliary law is not substituted for the root \(p\). The one-dimensional estimate gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{TV}(p,\widehat q)
&=\sum_i\alpha_i\operatorname{TV}(\rho^{(i)},\rho^{(i),\mathrm{can}})\\
&\ge\kappa-3\sum_i\max_jp_{(i,j)}
\ge\kappa-3(\omega+1)p_{\max}.
\end{aligned}
\]

To compare \(\widehat q\) with \(q^{\mathrm{can}}\), retain the full two-coordinate parity \(\mathbf B\). Write \(a_{i\mid\mathbf b}=\Pr(X_1=i\mid\mathbf B=\mathbf b)\). In the canonical endpoint law, conditional row pairs \((i,k)\) have probabilities \(a_{i\mid\mathbf b}a_{k\mid\mathbf b}\). In the auxiliary rowwise endpoint law, they have probabilities \(a_{i\mid\mathbf b}\) on \((i,i)\) and zero off the diagonal. Conditional on a fixed diagonal row pair and parity, the laws of the second-coordinate endpoints agree. Consequently the total variation between these endpoint laws is exactly

\[
\chi=\sum_{\mathbf b}\pi_{\mathbf b}
\left(1-\sum_i a_{i\mid\mathbf b}^2\right)
=\Pr(X_1\ne Y_1).
\]

Pushing forward to the midpoint gives \(\operatorname{TV}(q^{\mathrm{can}},\widehat q)\le\chi\). Since the first coordinates are integers,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\chi
&\le\mathbb E[(X_1-Y_1)^2]
=2\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid\mathbf B)\\
&=4\left(\mathbb E_pX_1^2-\mathbb E_{q^{\mathrm{can}}}J_1^2\right)
\le4\omega^2\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]

The final inequality uses that the function \(i\mapsto i^2\) has oscillation \(\omega^2\) on the common coordinate range. Thus the covariance decrement is used only for a bounded coarse coordinate, not to infer uniform integrability of an unbounded spatial moment. Combining the two total-variation comparisons proves \(\kappa-3(\omega+1)p_{\max}\le(1+4\omega^2)\delta\). If \(\omega\le1\), the first coordinate is determined by its parity, so \(\chi=0\), proving the improved denominator.

For completeness, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|v)\ge2\operatorname{TV}(u,v)^2\) for finite probability laws follows by grouping sites on which \(u>v\). The log-sum inequality reduces relative entropy to the binary relative entropy with mass difference \(\operatorname{TV}(u,v)\). For a fixed reference binary mass in \((0,1)\), its relative entropy as a function of the other mass has second derivative \(1/[t(1-t)]\ge4\), value zero and derivative zero at the reference mass. Integrating twice gives the claimed bound; endpoint cases follow by limits. Apply this with \(u=q^{\mathrm{can}},v=p\). If \(p_{\max}\le\kappa/[6(\omega+1)]\), the total-variation bound yields relative entropy at least \(\kappa^2/[2(1+4\omega^2)^2]\), strictly larger than \(\varepsilon_0(\omega)\). Its contrapositive and \(\sum p_{\mathbf I}^4\ge p_{\max}^4\) prove the stated atomic inverse for bounded width.

The canonical map has a global continuity bound that does not require parity masses to be bounded below. Namely, \(\operatorname{TV}(\mathcal T(p),\mathcal T(u))\le3\operatorname{TV}(p,u)\) for any finite probability laws on \(\mathbb Z^2\). To prove it, in each parity class write their unnormalized restrictions as \(\pi\mu\) and \(\sigma\nu\), with normalized conditional laws \(\mu,\nu\). When a mass is zero its conditional law may be chosen arbitrarily. The canonical endpoint laws in that class are \(\pi\mu\otimes\mu\) and \(\sigma\nu\otimes\nu\), and

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\pi\mu\otimes\mu-\sigma\nu\otimes\nu\|_1
&\le\pi\|\mu-\nu\|_1+\|\pi\mu-\sigma\nu\|_1\\
&\le2\|\pi\mu-\sigma\nu\|_1+|\pi-\sigma|.
\end{aligned}
\]

Sum over parity classes, use \(\sum|\pi-\sigma|\le\|p-u\|_1\), and push forward to the midpoint. This proves the continuity bound.

For the slab assertion, let \(u\) be \(p\) conditioned on \(A\), so \(\operatorname{TV}(p,u)=\eta\) and \(u_{\max}\le p_{\max}/(1-\eta)\). Its support remains complete: its convex hull lies in both \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\) and the slab, so every lattice point in that convex hull belongs to \(A\). It remains log-affine with the same tilt. A primitive \(\mathbf v\) extends to an integral basis by Bezout's identity; an integral affine lattice bijection therefore puts \(A\) in first-coordinate range zero through \(\omega\). The bounded-width result applies to this auxiliary \(u\). The continuity bound and the triangle inequality give

\[
\operatorname{TV}(u,\mathcal T(u))
\le\operatorname{TV}(u,p)+\delta+
\operatorname{TV}(\mathcal T(p),\mathcal T(u))
\le\delta+4\eta,
\]

which proves the claimed lower bound for the original root \(\delta\).

In a putative countersequence, \(p_{\max}\to0\), since \(p_{\max}^4\le\sum p_{\mathbf I}^4\); conversely \(\sum p_{\mathbf I}^4\le p_{\max}^3\). Also \(\delta\to0\) by the proved relative-entropy bound. Fix \(\omega\), write \(B_\omega=1+4\omega^2\), and suppose along infinitely many terms there is a slab with \(\eta\le\kappa/(16B_\omega)\). Then \(1-\eta\ge15/16\), and eventually \(3(\omega+1)p_{\max}/(1-\eta)\le\kappa/2\), uniformly over all those slabs. The slab bound gives \(\delta\ge\kappa/(2B_\omega)-4\eta\ge\kappa/(4B_\omega)>0\), a contradiction. If the minimum lattice width were bounded on a subsequence, the support itself would fit one of these slabs with \(\eta=0\). This proves the structural consequences.

Finally consider the displayed trapezoids. Their only integer first coordinates are zero and one, and their corresponding integer fibers are exactly \(0\le j\le M^2\) and \(0\le j\le M\). All four vertices are lattice points in the support; thus the convex hull is exactly the displayed polygon and the support is complete and rank two. The tilt \(\boldsymbol\theta=(2\log M,0)\) gives precisely the displayed positive root law and normalizer. Its row masses are \(\alpha_0=(M^2+1)/Z_M\) and \(\alpha_1=M^2(M+1)/Z_M\). Its largest atom is \(M^2/Z_M\to0\), and its original normalized fourth atomic moment is exactly

\[
64\sum_{\mathbf I}(p^{(M)}_{\mathbf I})^4
=64\frac{M^2+1+(M+1)M^8}{(M^3+2M^2+1)^4}\longrightarrow0.
\]

For a real linear functional \(\ell(x,y)=a x+b y\), put \(V_\ell=\mathbb E_p\operatorname{Var}(\ell(\mathbf X)\mid\mathbf X\bmod2)\). The parity determines \(x\) in this width-one family. Therefore, by conditional variance decomposition,

\[
V_\ell\le b^2\left(\alpha_0\operatorname{Var}(U_{M^2})+
\alpha_1\operatorname{Var}(U_M)\right)\le b^2M^3,
\]

where \(U_N\) is uniform on \(\{0,\ldots,N\}\). Indeed, \(\operatorname{Var}(U_N)=N(N+2)/12\le N^2/4\), \(\alpha_0\le2/M\), and \(\alpha_1\le1\).

The exact fourth centered moment of \(U_N\), obtained by expanding the finite sums of powers, is

\[
\mathbb E[(U_N-N/2)^4]
=\frac{N(N+2)(3N^2+6N-4)}{240}\ge\frac{N^4}{80}.
\]

Symmetry gives \(\mathbb E[(U_N-c)^4]=\mathbb E[(U_N-N/2)^4]+6(c-N/2)^2\operatorname{Var}(U_N)+(c-N/2)^4\). Thus the centered choice minimizes the fourth moment among all real centers. The contribution of row zero to the fourth moment of any centered \(\ell\) consequently gives, when \(b\ne0\),

\[
\mathbb E_p[(\ell(\mathbf X)-\mathbb E_p\ell(\mathbf X))^4]
\ge\frac{\alpha_0b^4M^8}{80}
\ge\frac{b^4M^7}{240}.
\]

Here \(Z_M\le3M^3\) for \(M\ge2\), so \(\alpha_0\ge1/(3M)\). The ratio in the statement is therefore at most \(240/M\), uniformly over \(a,b\) with \(b\ne0\). If \(b=0\) and \(\ell\) is nonconstant, its numerator is zero and its denominator is positive, so the same bound holds. This exactly refutes the uniform global projection-moment criterion. Nevertheless, the proved width-one estimate gives \(\operatorname{TV}(p^{(M)},\mathcal T(p^{(M)}))\ge\kappa-6M^2/Z_M\); the relative-entropy bound yields the asserted positive KL lower limit. All these calculations use the original root \(p^{(M)}\), not a row-conditioned replacement.
statement:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z^2\) be finite and nonempty, with \(D=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^2\), and let the original root law be \(p_{\mathbf I}=e^{\boldsymbol\theta\cdot\mathbf I}/Z>0\) on \(D\), extended by zero elsewhere. No integral-mean condition is imposed. The exact normalization map to accepted fact 464815b935df9890 is \(w=p\) and \(W=1\). Write \(p_{\max}=\max_Dp_{\mathbf I}\), and let \(\pi_{\mathbf b}=\sum_{\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2}p_{\mathbf I}\). The canonical array and its row law are

\[
r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}
=\frac{p_{\mathbf I}p_{2\mathbf J-\mathbf I}}{\pi_{\mathbf I\bmod2}},
\qquad
q^{\mathrm{can}}_{\mathbf J}
=\sum_{\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}.
\]

These are exactly the array \(r\) and row probability law \(q\) of accepted fact `464815b935df9890`. Write \(\mathcal T(p)=q^{\mathrm{can}}\). The notation \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}\) below means only the different, globally same-parity-conditioned midpoint law of accepted fact `3a28e7b649873797`. Write \(H(p)=-\sum p\log p\) for Shannon entropy; this is the quantity denoted \(S(p)\) in `464815b935df9890`, not its conditional assignment entropy \(H(r)\). The symbols \(C,S\) retain their locked-problem meanings. Every conditional row or slab law below is auxiliary: \(64\sum p_{\mathbf I}^4=8^2\sum p_{\mathbf I}^4\), and any use of the project's \(\tau\) or \(M_3\), retain the original root law \(p\).

Let \(\kappa\in(0,1]\) be precisely the one-dimensional separation constant in item 2 of accepted fact `3a28e7b649873797`, and put \(\delta=\operatorname{TV}(p,\mathcal T(p))\), with total variation normalized as one half of the \(\ell^1\) distance. The following assertions hold.

First, for any finitely supported probability law whose same-parity midpoints belong to its support, the canonical law is stationary if and only if the support contains at most one site in each parity class. The weights at these sites need not be equal. For the log-affine law above,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{q^{\mathrm{can}}}\mathbf J&=\mathbb E_p\mathbf X,\\
\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf X)-\operatorname{Cov}_{q^{\mathrm{can}}}(\mathbf J)
&=\frac12\sum_{\mathbf b}\pi_{\mathbf b}
\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf X\mid\mathbf X\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2),\\
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{\mathrm{can}}\|p)&=H(p)-H(q^{\mathrm{can}}).
\end{aligned}
\]

Second, suppose that an integral affine lattice bijection puts \(D\) in \(\{0,\ldots,\omega\}\times\mathbb Z\), where \(\omega\) is a nonnegative integer. Then

\[
\delta\ge
\frac{[\kappa-3(\omega+1)p_{\max}]_+}{1+4\omega^2},
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{\mathrm{can}}\|p)\ge2\delta^2.
\]

Here \([t]_+=\max\{t,0\}\). If \(\omega\le1\), the denominator \(1+4\omega^2\) in the total-variation bound can be omitted. In particular, for each fixed \(\omega\), the constants

\[
\varepsilon_0(\omega)=\frac{\kappa^2}{4(1+4\omega^2)^2},
\qquad
\kappa_0(\omega)=64\left(\frac{\kappa}{6(\omega+1)}\right)^4
\]

satisfy \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{\mathrm{can}}\|p)\le\varepsilon_0(\omega)\Rightarrow64\sum p_{\mathbf I}^4\ge\kappa_0(\omega)\).

More generally, let \(\mathbf v\in\mathbb Z^2\) be primitive, let \(a\in\mathbb Z\), and let \(A=\{\mathbf I\in D:a\le\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf I\le a+\omega\}\). If \(\eta=p(D\setminus A)<1\), then the original root law satisfies

\[
\delta\ge
\frac{\left[\kappa-\dfrac{3(\omega+1)p_{\max}}{1-\eta}\right]_+}{1+4\omega^2}
-4\eta.
\]

Consequently, if \(D^{(k)},p^{(k)}\) is any sequence of such planar root laws with \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal T(p^{(k)})\|p^{(k)})\to0\) and \(64\sum (p^{(k)}_{\mathbf I})^4\to0\), then for every fixed \(\omega\), eventually every primitive integer slab of width \(\omega\) has outside mass greater than \(\kappa/[16(1+4\omega^2)]\). In particular, their minimum lattice widths, defined as \(\min_{\mathbf v\in\mathbb Z^2\ \mathrm{primitive}}(\max_{\mathbf I\in D^{(k)}}\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf I-\min_{\mathbf I\in D^{(k)}}\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf I)\), tend to infinity.

Third, no positive absolute constant lower-bounds

\[
\sup_{\ell\ \mathrm{nonconstant}}
\frac{\left(\mathbb E_p\operatorname{Var}(\ell(\mathbf X)\mid\mathbf X\bmod2)\right)^2}
{\mathbb E_p[(\ell(\mathbf X)-\mathbb E_p\ell(\mathbf X))^4]}
\]

over these laws as \(p_{\max}\to0\). The supremum ranges over real linear functionals nonconstant on the support. This is a fourth spatial moment, not the normalized fourth atomic moment. An exact width-one counterfamily to this moment bound is, for integers \(M\ge2\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
D_M^{\mathrm{trap}}
&=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(0,M^2),(1,0),(1,M)\}\cap\mathbb Z^2,\\
Z_M&=M^3+2M^2+1,\\
p^{(M)}_{(0,j)}&=Z_M^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le M^2),\\
p^{(M)}_{(1,j)}&=M^2Z_M^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le M).
\end{aligned}
\]

The displayed supremum is at most \(240/M\) for this family, whereas \(64\sum(p^{(M)}_{\mathbf I})^4\to0\) and \(\liminf_M D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal T(p^{(M)})\|p^{(M)})\ge2\kappa^2>0\). Thus this family refutes the moment bridge, not the requested canonical KL separation.
